LSL: does the receiver keep up or let the queue grow?

Controlled per-sample cost; real transmission between LSL processes. Acquisition duration: 30, 40 s, depending on the scenario. Randomized order, seed 7301. 93 runs attempted; 135 stream measurements; 0 technical failures.

Acquisition machine: {"system": "Linux", "release": "6.14.0-37-generic", "architecture": "x86_64", "python": "3.13.3", "cpu_count": 16}. Python and operating system are recorded during acquisition; reanalysis on another machine does not change them.

23streams with growing queues
0streams with confirmed data loss
0streams stopped with pending data

1. The direct answer

The observed transition lies between loads 0.95 and 1.05. This range applies to this machine, duration and configuration; it is not a universal capacity limit. Load 1 means the processing budget already consumes the entire interarrival interval; reading, conversion and scheduling take additional time.

A growing queue means data arrive faster than they are processed. A larger buffer retains more data, but does not speed up the consumer. A smaller buffer may bound latency by discarding samples: low delay with loss is not success.

2. Watch the backlog build up

A rising queue during transmission means backlog is accumulating. A decline after the red line means pending data are being processed. The processed fraction trails the sent fraction when the consumer falls behind. Each line is an actual run, not an average that hides peaks.

Does adding streams affect those already active?

EEG: 512 Hz / 32 channels; EMG: 2000 Hz / 8 channels; IMU: 100 Hz / 9 channels. One consumer shares its time across streams; controlled cost of 400 µs per sample, with existing parameters held fixed. Each stream has its own curve and confidence interval. Streams from one run are not independent repetitions. Time plots use streams from the same representative run, without combining different runs.

Does the queue recover while transmission continues?

6/6 runs demonstrated recovery with a complete drain and no loss. Queue depth and delay must first exceed their baseline ranges during overload. The baseline reference is the 95th percentile of baseline-window medians. Queue depth and delay must both return to the reference + 50 ms and stay there for 2 s across consecutive windows, using window medians. Recovery must occur while transmission continues. Return time is the beginning of the first qualifying sequence; confirmation occurs only at its end. Time resolution is limited by the window width.

For incomplete runs, p99 covers processed samples only; unknown total loss is never replaced with zero.

Reconstruction: held values, availability and sample age

All streams use the same grid of 16384 Hz. Native acquisition rates are preserved. Samples within a batch share a read time: the causal curve shows the newest available sample, held until the next read, without inventing arrival times within the batch. The green curve accepts only samples whose age since acquisition is ≤250 ms; gray shows the last value even when stale. The offline curve may interpolate using later samples and does not represent real-time availability. Missing acquisition samples are not interpolated. Purple playback preserves all samples at their acquisition times shifted by the explicitly configured delay of 0.25 s: a batch that arrives after its playback deadline produces a gap. It simulates a playback buffer with native-rate sample holding; it is neither ideal band-limited reconstruction nor transport-delay removal. The instantaneous latest-value view may omit intermediate batch samples from the display only. This is a short channel-1 preview, not every waveform from the run.

4. Where does total delay come from?

Total = transmitter chunk formation and scheduling + transport/queue until read + batch processing. For each sample, total delay runs from acquisition timestamp to processing completion. p99 is the delay below which 99% of processed samples fall; maximum is the worst observed case. Components below are run-level means of per-run medians; they must not be added to obtain p99. If observation ends with pending data, p99 and maximum cover processed samples only; they do not summarize the unprocessed tail.

LoadnTX chunk/scheduling ms Transport/queue msBatch processing msTotal p99 ms

1615.5188.662.9451.8
1.05615.5934.666.01936.5

Added delay is the difference between the last and first valid production windows, not the sum of all sample delays. Queue ms/s measures how much additional signal time accumulates per wall-clock second. Drain time runs from the end of acquisition to the last processing completion; when incomplete, it is only the observed time, not the time needed to recover.

Nyquist and streams with different rates

Acquisition rate must exceed twice the highest signal frequency, with antialias filtering and a practical margin. This differs from the batch-reading frequency and display grid rate. A fast shared grid does not create new measurements in a slower stream. Offline interpolation cannot undo aliasing or prove real-time availability. Ideal rectangular marker pulses are not band-limited analog signals.

A shared consumer can delay EEG while processing EMG. In an application, separate reading from processing using bounded queues, preserve LSL timestamps and define an explicit sample-age/discard policy. Independent readers cannot fix insufficient consumer capacity; they only move the backlog elsewhere. This experiment keeps the shared consumer to measure competition between streams.

5. Statistical evidence and criteria

Prespecified primary comparison: loads ≥1 versus ≤0.9, paired by repetition. Difference in queue growth: 35.0 ms/s (95% bootstrap CI: 34.3 to 35.4); two-sided exact sign test p=0.03125, 6 complete pairs, 6 non-tied. The statistical unit is the run, never an individual sample. Exploratory intervals based on few repetitions are imprecise; other contrasts and the boundary are descriptive, without multiple significance claims.

Medians in windows of 1 s, excluding the first window and the entire drain phase. Sustained growth requires at least four windows, queue slope >10 ms/s and total-delay growth >50 ms. For recovery cases, slope and delay growth are calculated during overload only; the return diagnosis uses the sustained criterion shown in the recovery plot. The boundary requires growth in every repetition and a slope CI lower bound above 10 ms/s; the stable bound requires a CI upper bound ≤10 ms/s, with no loss or observation cutoffs.

Queue depth is the available-sample count reported by samples_available(), before reading and after processing. Sampled queue peaks may underestimate peaks between reads. This metric measures neither every internal buffer in bytes nor clock drift. Controlled processing cost is imposed by serial waiting; the experiment measures the consequence of insufficient capacity, not EEG-algorithm performance. Drain observation limit: 30 s, allowing an already-started batch to finish. If data remain at the limit, total loss is unknown. Latency uses the initial LSL clock correction and ends in the Python process, not at a hardware timestamp. Technical failures are never included in averages as zero.
